concepts.caption: An IOU: you lend, they pay interest, you get the principal back.
concepts.definition: A debt security issued by a government or company, paying interest and repaying principal at maturity.
concepts.example: The benchmark 6.94% 2036 bond settled at 7.4427%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A bond is the certificate; yield is the return it pays at the price you paid.

concepts.caption: The interest rate printed on the certificate, paid on face value.
concepts.definition: The fixed annual interest rate on a bond's face value, regardless of what it trades at.
concepts.example: The security carries a coupon of 6.94% and matures in 2036.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The coupon is fixed on face value; yield moves with the price you paid. Buy at a discount and the yield exceeds the coupon.

concepts.caption: The date on the certificate when the principal comes back.
concepts.definition: The date the principal is due, or the time remaining until that date.
concepts.example: Its principal is repaid at maturity, while the coupon is paid semi-annually.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Maturity is a date on the calendar; duration is how sensitive the price is to rates, usually shorter than maturity.

concepts.caption: The money lent, to be repaid at the end.
concepts.definition: The face value of a bond — the amount the issuer repays at maturity.
concepts.example: Inflation-linked bonds adjust principal for the consumer price index.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Principal is the amount returned; the coupon is the interest paid along the way.

concepts.caption: What the bond pays you at the price you paid for it.
concepts.definition: Investment return relative to price; bond yields rise when prices fall.
concepts.example: Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Yield floats with price; the coupon is fixed on the certificate.

concepts.caption: What the certificate costs in the market right now.
concepts.definition: The secondary-market price of a bond, usually quoted as a percentage of face value.
concepts.example: The benchmark bond settled at 7.4427%, compared with 7.3920% on Monday.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Price and yield move in opposite directions. See one and you should already know which way the other went.

concepts.caption: How far the price moves when rates move.
concepts.definition: A measure of a bond's price sensitivity to rate changes, in years, usually shorter than maturity.
concepts.example: A portfolio with an average duration of seven years loses roughly 7% for a one-point rise.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Duration is sensitivity; maturity is a date. They are equal only for zero-coupon bonds.

concepts.caption: The issue everyone else is priced against.
concepts.definition: A specific bond or index used as the reference for pricing, such as the ten-year government bond.
concepts.example: The benchmark yield settled at 7.4427%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A benchmark is the one chosen as the reference; a bond is any issue.

concepts.caption: One hundredth of a percent — the standard unit for rate moves.
concepts.definition: The smallest common unit for quoting rate changes: one basis point is 0.01%.
concepts.example: Swap markets are pricing in about 100 basis points of rate increases.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A basis point is a unit of measurement; the policy rate is the level being measured.

concepts.caption: The highest yield accepted when the auction clears.
concepts.definition: The yield corresponding to the lowest price the issuer accepts in an auction, setting the actual cost of borrowing.
concepts.example: A weak bid-to-cover forces the central bank to accept a higher cut-off yield.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The cut-off yield is the result of one auction; yield is the market level at any moment.

concepts.caption: Principal or coupon adjusts with the price index.
concepts.definition: A bond whose principal or interest is adjusted for inflation, hedging rising prices.
concepts.example: Inflation-linked bonds, whose principal is adjusted for the consumer price index, drew strong demand.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Inflation-linked principal moves with prices; a fixed-rate bond pins both coupon and principal.

concepts.caption: One rate for the whole life of the bond.
concepts.definition: A bond or loan whose coupon is set at issue and never changes until maturity.
concepts.example: The corporate bond market priced a large fixed-rate issue at a spread of 180 basis points.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Fixed-rate is locked; floating-rate resets against a benchmark.

concepts.caption: The rate resets against a benchmark, so it moves.
concepts.definition: A bond or loan whose coupon resets periodically at a benchmark plus a fixed margin.
concepts.example: Floating-rate notes attracted buyers expecting the policy rate to keep rising.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Floating-rate moves with the benchmark; fixed-rate never changes.

concepts.caption: Governments and companies sell bonds by competitive bidding.
concepts.definition: Issuing bonds through a competitive bidding process.
concepts.example: The government's borrowing programme relies on regular auctions.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An auction is the bidding process; issuance is the act of bringing the bonds out.

concepts.caption: The amount of new debt brought to market.
concepts.definition: The act, or total volume, of issuing new securities.
concepts.example: Primary dealers must absorb unsold supply when issuance is heavy.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Issuance is the volume; an auction is the event where it gets priced.

concepts.caption: How many bids came in for each bond actually sold.
concepts.definition: Total bids received divided by the amount issued — a gauge of auction demand.
concepts.example: Dealers watch the bid-to-cover ratio to gauge demand.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Bid-to-cover measures how hot demand was; the cut-off yield is what that demand cost the issuer.

concepts.caption: An institution obliged to bid at every auction.
concepts.definition: A firm authorised to deal directly with the issuer and required to bid in auctions.
concepts.example: Primary dealers are required to bid at every auction and absorb unsold supply.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A primary dealer is a participant; bid-to-cover is the outcome of the auction.

concepts.caption: Central-government debt, the highest credit there is.
concepts.definition: Debt issued by a central government, generally treated as the risk-free benchmark.
concepts.example: India's overnight indexed swap rates rose in line with Treasury yields.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Treasury usually means US government debt; a gilt is specifically British.

concepts.caption: British government debt, named for the gilded edge on old certificates.
concepts.definition: A British government bond, traditionally regarded as very high credit quality.
concepts.example: UK gilt investors expect the budget to pass without market drama.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Gilts are specifically British; treasury is the general term for central-government debt.

concepts.caption: Debt backed by a state, whichever state it is.
concepts.definition: Debt issued by a sovereign government — the category covering all central-government bonds.
concepts.example: The sovereign yield curve has climbed sharply.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Sovereign is the category — backed by state credit; treasury and gilt name particular countries' versions.

concepts.caption: A company's debt, usually paying more than government debt.
concepts.definition: A debt security issued by a non-government company.
concepts.example: The corporate bond market priced a large fixed-rate issue at a spread of 180 basis points.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Corporate bonds carry company credit; sovereigns carry state credit. The company pays more.

concepts.caption: Short-term corporate IOUs, usually months not years.
concepts.definition: Unsecured short-term debt issued by companies, typically under a year.
concepts.example: Foreign holdings of onshore bonds remained unchanged, and commercial paper demand held up.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Commercial paper is short (under a year) and usually unsecured; corporate bonds are long and may be secured.

concepts.caption: Low-rated debt: high yield, high default risk.
concepts.definition: A bond rated below investment grade, also called high yield.
concepts.example: A junk bond sale was pulled after investors asked for a spread beyond the issuer's target.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Junk sits below the ratings line; investment grade sits above it.

concepts.caption: High enough rated that institutions can hold it.
concepts.definition: Debt rated at or above the investment-grade threshold, usually BBB-/Baa3.
concepts.example: Investment grade issuers still found buyers, but a junk sale was pulled.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Investment grade is above the line; junk is below it.

concepts.caption: Every maturity's yield joined into one line.
concepts.definition: Yields across maturities plotted together, showing what the market expects rates to do.
concepts.example: The sovereign yield curve has climbed sharply.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A yield is one point at one maturity; the yield curve is the shape of all of them.

concepts.caption: The extra yield a company pays over the government.
concepts.definition: The gap between a corporate bond's yield and a government bond of the same maturity — the price of credit risk.
concepts.example: Investors demanded a spread of 180 basis points over the comparable government security.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A credit spread pays for credit risk; a term premium pays for time. Both lift long yields, separately.

concepts.caption: That extra yield grew — the market got more worried.
concepts.definition: Credit spreads expanding, usually meaning investors demand more compensation for risk.
concepts.example: The spread widening was most visible at the long end.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Widening means more worry; tightening means less.

concepts.caption: That extra yield shrank — the market relaxed.
concepts.definition: Credit spreads narrowing, usually meaning improved risk appetite.
concepts.example: Spread tightening in high-grade names contrasted with widening in lower-rated credit.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Tightening means less worry; widening means more.

concepts.caption: The extra you get paid for locking money up for longer.
concepts.definition: The additional yield investors demand for holding a long bond instead of rolling short ones.
concepts.example: The term premium has risen as supply grows.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The term premium pays for time; a credit spread pays for credit risk. Both lift long yields, for different reasons.

concepts.caption: Short yields above long — the curve bends down.
concepts.definition: An unusual shape where short maturities yield more than long ones, historically a warning of slowdown.
concepts.example: Curve inversion has deepened: the two-year now yields more than the ten-year.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Inversion is one specific shape of the curve; the yield curve is the curve itself.

concepts.caption: The chance the borrower does not pay you back.
concepts.definition: The likelihood a borrower fails to pay interest or repay principal on time.
concepts.example: Default risk for the weaker issuers is now priced explicitly.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Default risk is the actual likelihood; a credit rating is an agency's score for it.

concepts.caption: An agency's score for how likely you are to be repaid.
concepts.definition: An assessment of an issuer's ability to repay, graded from AAA down to D.
concepts.example: The sovereign's credit rating was left unchanged, with the outlook stable.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A rating is the score; default risk is the thing being scored.

concepts.caption: The agency moved the rating down a notch.
concepts.definition: A ratings agency lowering an issuer's or bond's credit rating.
concepts.example: A downgrade would raise refinancing costs for the corporate sector too.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A downgrade moves down; an upgrade moves up.

concepts.caption: The agency moved the rating up a notch.
concepts.definition: A ratings agency raising an issuer's or bond's credit rating.
concepts.example: The agencies left the rating unchanged, though an upgrade was possible later.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An upgrade moves up; a downgrade moves down.

concepts.caption: A clause in the paperwork restricting what the borrower may do.
concepts.definition: A term in a bond or loan agreement limiting the borrower's behaviour, such as further borrowing.
concepts.example: Covenants on the new issues restrict additional borrowing.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A covenant restricts what the borrower does; refinancing replaces old debt with new. Covenants often get renegotiated during refinancing.

concepts.caption: Borrowing again to pay off what is already due.
concepts.definition: Repaying existing debt with the proceeds of newly issued debt.
concepts.example: Several issuers have begun refinancing existing debt to push out maturities.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Refinancing is the purpose (replace old debt); issuance is the act. Refinancing always involves issuance, but not the reverse.

concepts.caption: The rate the central bank sets.
concepts.definition: The target rate set by a central bank to steer market rates.
concepts.example: The central bank raised the policy rate earlier this month.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The policy rate is the level; a basis point is the unit used to measure moves in it.

concepts.caption: The reference rate floating products are priced off.
concepts.definition: A reference rate used to price other instruments, such as SOFR or OIS.
concepts.example: Floating-rate notes are priced at a spread over a benchmark rate.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A benchmark rate is the market's pricing reference (like SOFR); the policy rate is what the central bank targets. The first follows the second but is not the same thing.
